* ares_cancel/ares_destroy: detach queries before running user callbacks

Both functions release each still-running query themselves rather than
going through end_query().  Claiming the list node unlinks the query from
all_queries only -- it stays in queries_by_qid, on conn->queries_to_conn
and in queries_by_timeout for the whole duration of the callback.

A reentrant teardown from inside that callback therefore still finds the
query and ends it a second time, invoking the application callback twice
for one lookup and freeing it; the ares_free_query() that follows then
double-frees.  Two ordinary things reach it: ares_set_servers_csv(), which
closes the connections of servers that are no longer configured, and
starting a replacement lookup whose write fails.  One query in flight is
enough.

This is the ordering rule ares_flush_requeue() already follows on the
response path.  It was applied there and never to these two.

Both loops also cached the next node across the callback, which a nested
teardown can free.  Re-read the head each iteration instead, the idiom
already used by ares_destroy_servers_state() and ares_close_sockets().

ares_send_nolock() now refuses new queries once channel->sys_up is clear.
ares_destroy(3) already documents that a callback must not add requests to
a channel being destroyed, and without this a callback that starts a
replacement lookup on every invocation keeps ares_destroy() spinning: each
new query lands on the list being drained.  The request is refused and the
caller's callback is invoked with ARES_EDESTRUCTION so it can release
whatever it attached -- but only when not already inside such a
notification, since a callback that retries on failure would otherwise
re-enter without bound and exhaust the stack.  Internal requeues are unaffected -- they
go through ares_send_query_int(), not ares_send_nolock() -- so
ares_close_sockets() still requeues correctly during teardown.

ares_detach_query() becomes non-static and is declared in ares_private.h,
since both files now need it.

Tests: four covering both functions, both triggers, and the cached-next
pointer.  All fail on unpatched source under ASAN -- three with
"attempting double-free", one with heap-use-after-free in
ares_llist_node_next().  Each asserts its lookup is notified exactly once,
so a duplicate notification is caught as well as the free.

* ares_process: fix double-free and UAF in the synchronous query-completion path

end_query() has a synchronous branch, taken when requeue is NULL, that
invoked the query callback while the query was still linked in
channel->all_queries and channel->queries_by_qid, then freed it. A
reentrant ares_cancel() from that callback found the same query, freed
it, and the ares_free_query() below double-freed it. Detach before the
callback, matching what ares_flush_requeue() already does on the
deferred path (CVE-2026-33630).

Fixing the sink rather than its callers covers both routes that reach
it with a NULL requeue:

  - connection teardown:
    handle_conn_error() -> ares_close_connection() -> ares_requeue_queries()
  - server removal:
    ares_set_servers_csv() -> ares_servers_update()
      -> ares_servers_remove_stale() -> ares_slist_node_destroy()
      -> server_destroy_cb() -> ares_destroy_server() -> ares_close_sockets()
      -> ares_close_connection()

The second route is easy to miss: reconfiguring can also shrink
max_tries (servers * tries), so an in-flight query can find itself past
its retry limit as a side effect of the reconfiguration itself.

Separately, ares_send_query_int() called handle_conn_error() and then
kept using its own query pointer. That teardown can terminally end other
queries on the same connection, and a reentrant ares_cancel() from one
of their callbacks frees this query too -- it is still linked in
all_queries, since it only joins conn->queries_to_conn on the success
path further down. Re-check liveness via the qid captured at entry
before requeueing, mirroring the guard in ares_send_query(). This one is
masked while the double-free above is unfixed, since that aborts first.

ares_detach_query() now only releases the query-ID slot when it still holds
this query.  Detaching before a callback opens a window in which a lookup
started from inside that callback can be issued the same id, and the
ares_free_query() below detaches a second time -- which would otherwise
evict the new lookup from queries_by_qid, leaving its response unmatchable.
Pre-existing in ares_flush_requeue(); this branch adds a third site and the
cancel/destroy branch adds two more, so the fix belongs in the shared

* ares_conn: defer socket-state notifications to a safe point

ares_conn_sock_state_cb_update() dispatched the application's socket-state
callback from the middle of opening, writing to or closing a connection, and
every caller keeps using that connection afterwards.  That callback is
registered with ARES_OPT_SOCK_STATE_CB and is how c-ares is normally driven
from an event loop, so it is widely used.

A reentrant call from it frees the connection by two separate routes:
ares_cancel() through the idle-connection sweep, and ares_set_servers_csv()
by destroying the server that owns it.  It also frees the in-flight query.

Queue the notification and deliver it once no frame still holds the
connection, rather than dispatching inline and trying to suppress the ways
it can be freed.  Suppressing the sweep covered only the first route, and
left the sweep never re-running: the application was told to watch a socket
and never told to stop, while ares_getsock() reported nothing outstanding.

Only the descriptor and the state are captured, never the connection, and
insertion order is preserved, so an application observes the same sequence
of state changes it would have seen inline -- and always before the outermost
c-ares call returns.  A call made from within a callback is not the outermost
one, so what it produces arrives after that call has returned.

Delivery is bracketed at every public entry point that can close a
connection: ares_process_fds_nolock(), ares_send_nolock(), ares_cancel(),
ares_servers_update() and the server teardown in ares_destroy().  Covering
only the first two silently dropped the rest.  ares_destroy() delivers
rather than discarding, since applications rely on those closures to
deregister descriptors from their own event loop.

The region primitive is named for what it is rather than for one callback
kind -- ares_deferred_cb_enter()/ares_deferred_cb_leave() over a single
channel->deferred_cb_depth -- so the server-state deferral that follows in
this series folds onto it instead of building a second copy.  The
dispatch counts as a nesting level of its own, so a callback that re-enters
the library cannot drain and destroy the queue underneath the loop, nor
have its next notification delivered from inside the current one.

ares_send_query_int() also re-checks its query after the two places that run
application code: ares_open_connection(), which runs the socket-open function
and the socket-create and socket-configure callbacks, and
ares_conn_query_write(), which runs the application's send function.  With the
notification queued neither can reach the socket-state callback any more, but
any of those can still reentrantly call ares_cancel().  Each re-check is
independently necessary.

docs/ares_init_options.3 documents the guarantee and the delivery ordering
under ARES_OPT_SOCK_STATE_CB, including that ares_destroy() reports the
closure of every socket it still holds before returning.

* ares_process: defer server-state notifications to a safe point

server_increment_failures() and server_set_good() dispatched the
application's server-state callback as their last action, and all six
callers kept using their query afterwards: process_timeouts(),
process_answer() on both the error and valid-response paths,
handle_conn_error(), and ares_send_query_int() twice.

Nothing documents that callback as non-reentrant and the channel lock is
recursive, so an application cancelling from it left the library
dereferencing a freed query.  An ordinary timeout reaches it; no hostile
input is required.

Queue the notifications and dispatch them once the work that produced them
is finished, rather than adding a liveness re-check at each site.  Six
sites is already enough for one to be missed, and a new caller would have
to remember.

This reuses the deferred-callback region introduced for socket-state
notifications in the preceding commit rather than building a second copy of
it: one channel->deferred_cb_depth, one enter/leave pair per entry point,
and one flush that drains both queues.  Dispatch is gated on that nesting
depth rather than on particular call sites being outermost, so a future
nested caller cannot reintroduce the problem.  Only the formatted server
address is captured, never the ares_server_t, so a queued entry cannot
outlive anything it points at.

At teardown the queue is delivered rather than dropped, for the same reason
the socket-state queue is: the notification is the application's, and
ares_destroy() is where it stops being able to ask for it.  Delivery runs
after the servers are destroyed rather than before -- that step requeues
queries through ares_close_connection(), which can reach
server_increment_failures() and queue more.

docs/ares_set_server_state_callback.3 gains a REENTRANCY section covering
the guarantee, the delivery timing, and which callback receives a queued
notification.  docs/ares_cancel.3 gains the matching guarantee for
callbacks it invokes, which was relied on but never written down.

Two places kept using an ares_server_t after the application had caused it
to be released by reconfiguring the server list from inside a callback.

never was.  Only one site records a server at all: the EDNS fallback taken

* review round 5: bound shutdown refusal, revalidate servers, key liveness on serial

Three findings from review of the consolidated series, plus three comment
and formatting corrections.

The refusal added for a channel being destroyed invoked the application
callback unconditionally.  An application whose callback responds to failure
by starting a replacement lookup -- an ordinary retry pattern, since
ARES_EDESTRUCTION is just another failure status -- re-entered the refusal
from inside the notification without bound and exhausted the stack, roughly
ten thousand frames in.  Notify only when not already inside such a
notification, which bounds it at one frame.  A nested request's argument is
no longer handed back; ares_destroy.3 says so rather than promising the
notification unconditionally.

ares_send_query_int() re-checked its query after ares_open_connection() but
not the server it captured beforehand, and the same three pieces of
application code that can free the query can free the server:
ares_set_servers_csv() from any of them destroys the servers the new
configuration omits.  Revalidate the server there, and inside
ares_open_connection() after its own two callbacks, where conn->server is
dereferenced immediately afterwards by ares_conn_set_self_ip().
ares_server_in_channel() becomes non-static for the second site.

The liveness guards tested a query id plus pointer identity.  That has the
residual case the serial was introduced to remove -- a replacement lookup is
often allocated at the address the freed one had, and may be handed the same
16-bit id -- so they now compare query->serial through a single
ares_query_is_live() helper.  The pre-existing id check at the end of
ares_send_query() gets the same treatment; it previously tested only for
NULL, so a reissued id made it report success for a query that had ended.

above already flushed and freed both queues; five overlapping comment blocks
in the test file are collapsed to the one that is true; and the test's
errno/fcntl includes no longer nest a _WIN32 guard inside a WIN32 one.

* defer reclamation of servers and connections across library calls

Six Majors across three review rounds, and three published CVEs before them,
are one defect: a library-owned object freed by application code while the
library still holds a pointer to it.  CVE-2025-31498 fixed it at one call
site; CVE-2025-62408 was "a missed case from CVE-2025-31498"; CVE-2026-33630
covered "the remaining occurrences of the pattern" for queries.  The server
and connection half has never had a mechanism, only point guards, and each
round of review has found another site.

Callbacks split cleanly in two.  Notification callbacks -- the query
callback, socket-state and server-state -- return nothing the library needs,
so their delivery is already deferred to a safe point, and that half has
produced no findings since.  The I/O hooks -- the socket-open function from
ares_set_socket_functions_ex(), and the ares_set_socket_callback() and
ares_set_socket_configure_callback() callbacks -- cannot be deferred, because
their return value is needed to continue.  They run inside half-constructed
state and may reconfigure the servers, which frees them.

So defer the destruction instead of the call.  ares_close_connection() and
ares_destroy_server() still unlink from every lookup structure immediately --
nothing can find a torn-down object, ares_server_in_channel() reports it gone
and ares_slist_node_find() does not return it -- but while a library call is
in progress the memory is put on a pending list and freed by the flush that
already delivers deferred notifications, once the outermost call is
unwinding.  A pointer captured before a hook therefore stays readable for the
rest of that call.

The existing revalidation checks stay, because they are still needed for
semantics: a removed server must not be selected, written to or have its
failure count adjusted.  What changes is that missing one is now "acted on a
server that was removed" rather than a use-after-free.

Teardown becomes idempotent.  Once a connection can outlive its own close,
reaching ares_close_connection() twice is ordinary -- handle_conn_error()
after a failed write does exactly that -- and doing the work twice would
requeue queries that have already moved and put the connection on the pending
list a second time, which is a double free.  ARES_CONN_FLAG_DEAD makes the
second call a no-op.  This was found by testing this change, not by review.

Verified with three reproducers using only the public API, under
AddressSanitizer, each run with reclamation enabled and disabled:

  configure hook reconfigures servers   ares_conn_connect()      UAF -> clean
  send function reconfigures servers    handle_conn_error()      UAF -> clean
  socket-create hook reconfigures       ares_conn_set_self_ip()  UAF -> clean

Test: ReconfigureInConfigureHookNoUseAfterFree, which is a heap-use-after-free
in ares_conn_connect() with reclamation disabled.  It also asserts the query
completes rather than being stranded.

Known limit: this protects payloads, not container nodes.  ares_slist_node_
destroy() still frees the node, so the re-read-the-head iteration discipline
and the servers_generation counter remain necessary.

* review round 7: harden teardown ordering, fix a leak, correct docs

The idempotence flag is set as soon as the connection is unlinked rather than
at the end of teardown.  ares_requeue_queries() runs in between and ends
queries terminally once their retries are exhausted, which invokes the
application's callback; with the flag set afterwards, a second
ares_close_connection() arriving in that window would run the body again,
close the descriptor twice and list the connection for reclamation twice.
Not reachable today -- after the unlink nothing can obtain the connection but
frames already on the stack, which run later -- but it now holds by
construction.  It also gives ares_close_sockets() its termination condition:
that loop re-reads the head and relies on the close unlinking the node, so a
dead connection on the list would spin with the channel lock held.  Asserted.

Restore the two queue destroys in ares_destroy().  They were removed as
redundant, and that was wrong for one path: if the first insert into a
freshly created queue fails, the array is left allocated and empty, the flush
loop never runs because both queues are empty, and nothing else frees it.
The suite drives allocation failure and CI runs it under valgrind.

CVE-2026-33630.1fa3b86a0b8d18fe7b60f3228a01d770feb026bc:
Merge commit from fork

* Fix double-free in process_timeouts() when ares_cancel() called from callback

Detach query from queries_by_qid and all_queries before invoking
callback to prevent ares_cancel() from finding and double-freeing it.

This applies the same requeue pattern used in read_answers() to
process_timeouts().

* Consolidate requeue handling: fix #1043 recursion and complete the double-free fix

The prior commit fixed the process_timeouts() double-free (GHSA-6wfj-rwm7-3542 /
CVE-2026-33630) by deferring callbacks and detaching the query before invoking
it.  However:

  1. The identical double-free is reachable through read_answers(): its deferred
     ENDQUERY flush invoked the callback without first detaching the query from
     queries_by_qid / all_queries, so a reentrant ares_cancel() from a *normal*
     response callback frees the query and read_answers() frees it again.  The
     advisory's premise that read_answers() was already safe holds only for
     cross-query cancellation, not self-cancellation.

  2. Issue #1043 (unbounded ares_requeue_query() -> ares_send_query() recursion
     leading to stack overflow) was still present: ares_send_query() and the
     read_answers()/process_timeouts() flushes re-dispatched retries by calling
     ares_send_query() directly rather than iteratively.

Both problems share one root cause: work that must be deferred was instead done
immediately.  This change funnels every flush site through a single helper,
ares_flush_requeue(), which:

  - re-dispatches retries by appending to the same list and looping (via the new
    internal ares_send_query_int()), so retryable failures iterate instead of
    recursing, and
  - fully detaches each query (ares_detach_query()) before invoking its callback,
    so a reentrant ares_cancel() can never find and double-free it.

ares_send_query() becomes a thin wrapper that drives ares_send_query_int() and
drains the list.  Because a deferred retry can terminally fail (and free the
query) while draining, the wrapper reports the query's real fate by checking
whether it is still tracked, rather than dereferencing the possibly-freed query.

read_answers(), process_timeouts(), and process_answer()'s EDNS-rewrite-failure
path now all defer through this helper, removing two duplicated inline flush
loops.

Regression tests (test/ares-test-mock.cc):
  - HighRetryNoStackOverflow: a large retry count with always-failing socket
    creation overflows the stack on unpatched code and completes iteratively
    with the fix.
  - CancelInCallbackNoDoubleFree: calling ares_cancel() from a normal response
    callback double-frees on unpatched code (ASan) and is clean with the fix.

* ares_conn: defer socket-state notifications to a safe point

ares_conn_sock_state_cb_update() dispatched the application's socket-state
callback from the middle of opening, writing to or closing a connection, and
every caller keeps using that connection afterwards.  That callback is
registered with ARES_OPT_SOCK_STATE_CB and is how c-ares is normally driven
from an event loop, so it is widely used.

A reentrant call from it frees the connection by two separate routes:
ares_cancel() through the idle-connection sweep, and ares_set_servers_csv()
by destroying the server that owns it.  It also frees the in-flight query.

Queue the notification and deliver it once no frame still holds the
connection, rather than dispatching inline and trying to suppress the ways
it can be freed.  Suppressing the sweep covered only the first route, and
left the sweep never re-running: the application was told to watch a socket
and never told to stop, while ares_getsock() reported nothing outstanding.

Only the descriptor and the state are captured, never the connection, and
insertion order is preserved, so an application observes the same sequence
of state changes it would have seen inline -- and always before the outermost
c-ares call returns.  A call made from within a callback is not the outermost
one, so what it produces arrives after that call has returned.

Delivery is bracketed at every public entry point that can close a
connection: ares_process_fds_nolock(), ares_send_nolock(), ares_cancel(),
ares_servers_update() and the server teardown in ares_destroy().  Covering
only the first two silently dropped the rest.  ares_destroy() delivers
rather than discarding, since applications rely on those closures to
deregister descriptors from their own event loop.

The region primitive is named for what it is rather than for one callback
kind -- ares_deferred_cb_enter()/ares_deferred_cb_leave() over a single
channel->deferred_cb_depth -- so the server-state deferral that follows in
this series folds onto it instead of building a second copy.  The
dispatch counts as a nesting level of its own, so a callback that re-enters
the library cannot drain and destroy the queue underneath the loop, nor
have its next notification delivered from inside the current one.

ares_send_query_int() also re-checks its query after the two places that run
application code: ares_open_connection(), which runs the socket-open function
and the socket-create and socket-configure callbacks, and
ares_conn_query_write(), which runs the application's send function.  With the
notification queued neither can reach the socket-state callback any more, but
any of those can still reentrantly call ares_cancel().  Each re-check is
independently necessary.

* defer reclamation of servers and connections across library calls

Six Majors across three review rounds, and three published CVEs before them,
are one defect: a library-owned object freed by application code while the
library still holds a pointer to it.  CVE-2025-31498 fixed it at one call
site; CVE-2025-62408 was "a missed case from CVE-2025-31498"; CVE-2026-33630
covered "the remaining occurrences of the pattern" for queries.  The server
and connection half has never had a mechanism, only point guards, and each
round of review has found another site.

Callbacks split cleanly in two.  Notification callbacks -- the query
callback, socket-state and server-state -- return nothing the library needs,
so their delivery is already deferred to a safe point, and that half has
produced no findings since.  The I/O hooks -- the socket-open function from
ares_set_socket_functions_ex(), and the ares_set_socket_callback() and
ares_set_socket_configure_callback() callbacks -- cannot be deferred, because
their return value is needed to continue.  They run inside half-constructed
state and may reconfigure the servers, which frees them.

So defer the destruction instead of the call.  ares_close_connection() and
ares_destroy_server() still unlink from every lookup structure immediately --
nothing can find a torn-down object, ares_server_in_channel() reports it gone
and ares_slist_node_find() does not return it -- but while a library call is
in progress the memory is put on a pending list and freed by the flush that
already delivers deferred notifications, once the outermost call is
unwinding.  A pointer captured before a hook therefore stays readable for the
rest of that call.

The existing revalidation checks stay, because they are still needed for
semantics: a removed server must not be selected, written to or have its
failure count adjusted.  What changes is that missing one is now "acted on a
server that was removed" rather than a use-after-free.

Teardown becomes idempotent.  Once a connection can outlive its own close,
reaching ares_close_connection() twice is ordinary -- handle_conn_error()
after a failed write does exactly that -- and doing the work twice would
requeue queries that have already moved and put the connection on the pending
list a second time, which is a double free.  ARES_CONN_FLAG_DEAD makes the
second call a no-op.  This was found by testing this change, not by review.

Verified with three reproducers using only the public API, under
AddressSanitizer, each run with reclamation enabled and disabled:

  configure hook reconfigures servers   ares_conn_connect()      UAF -> clean
  send function reconfigures servers    handle_conn_error()      UAF -> clean
  socket-create hook reconfigures       ares_conn_set_self_ip()  UAF -> clean

Queue the notification and deliver it once no frame still holds the
connection, rather than dispatching inline and trying to suppress the ways
it can be freed.  Suppressing the sweep covered only the first route, and
left the sweep never re-running: the application was told to watch a socket
and never told to stop, while ares_getsock() reported nothing outstanding.

Only the descriptor and the state are captured, never the connection, and
insertion order is preserved, so an application observes the same sequence
of state changes it would have seen inline -- and always before the outermost
c-ares call returns.  A call made from within a callback is not the outermost
one, so what it produces arrives after that call has returned.

Delivery is bracketed at every public entry point that can close a
connection: ares_process_fds_nolock(), ares_send_nolock(), ares_cancel(),
ares_servers_update() and the server teardown in ares_destroy().  Covering
only the first two silently dropped the rest.  ares_destroy() delivers
rather than discarding, since applications rely on those closures to
deregister descriptors from their own event loop.

The region primitive is named for what it is rather than for one callback
kind -- ares_deferred_cb_enter()/ares_deferred_cb_leave() over a single
channel->deferred_cb_depth -- so the server-state deferral that follows in
this series folds onto it instead of building a second copy.  The
dispatch counts as a nesting level of its own, so a callback that re-enters
the library cannot drain and destroy the queue underneath the loop, nor
have its next notification delivered from inside the current one.

ares_send_query_int() also re-checks its query after the two places that run
application code: ares_open_connection(), which runs the socket-open function
and the socket-create and socket-configure callbacks, and
ares_conn_query_write(), which runs the application's send function.  With the
notification queued neither can reach the socket-state callback any more, but
any of those can still reentrantly call ares_cancel().  Each re-check is
independently necessary.

docs/ares_init_options.3 documents the guarantee and the delivery ordering
under ARES_OPT_SOCK_STATE_CB, including that ares_destroy() reports the
closure of every socket it still holds before returning.

* ares_process: defer server-state notifications to a safe point

server_increment_failures() and server_set_good() dispatched the
application's server-state callback as their last action, and all six
callers kept using their query afterwards: process_timeouts(),
process_answer() on both the error and valid-response paths,
handle_conn_error(), and ares_send_query_int() twice.

Nothing documents that callback as non-reentrant and the channel lock is
recursive, so an application cancelling from it left the library
dereferencing a freed query.  An ordinary timeout reaches it; no hostile
input is required.

Queue the notifications and dispatch them once the work that produced them
is finished, rather than adding a liveness re-check at each site.  Six
sites is already enough for one to be missed, and a new caller would have
to remember.

This reuses the deferred-callback region introduced for socket-state
notifications in the preceding commit rather than building a second copy of
it: one channel->deferred_cb_depth, one enter/leave pair per entry point,
and one flush that drains both queues.  Dispatch is gated on that nesting
depth rather than on particular call sites being outermost, so a future
nested caller cannot reintroduce the problem.  Only the formatted server
address is captured, never the ares_server_t, so a queued entry cannot
outlive anything it points at.

At teardown the queue is delivered rather than dropped, for the same reason
the socket-state queue is: the notification is the application's, and
ares_destroy() is where it stops being able to ask for it.  Delivery runs
after the servers are destroyed rather than before -- that step requeues
queries through ares_close_connection(), which can reach
server_increment_failures() and queue more.

the guarantee, the delivery timing, and which callback receives a queued
notification.  docs/ares_cancel.3 gains the matching guarantee for
callbacks it invokes, which was relied on but never written down.

timeout.  Both fail on unpatched source under ASAN with heap-use-after-free

Two places kept using an ares_server_t after the application had caused it
to be released by reconfiguring the server list from inside a callback.

Deferred requeue entries record the query by qid and the server by raw
pointer.  On drain the query is re-looked-up -- precisely because a
callback earlier in the same drain may have cancelled it -- but the server
never was.  Only one site records a server at all: the EDNS fallback taken
when a server answers FORMERR without an OPT record, which requeues to that
same server to retry without EDNS.  Check the server is still in the
channel's list before using it, and fall back to ordinary selection if not.
The check compares pointers and never dereferences the candidate, since it
may already be freed and ares_slist_node_find() would read through it via
the sort callback.

removal instead.

* review round 5: bound shutdown refusal, revalidate servers, key liveness on serial

Three findings from review of the consolidated series, plus three comment
and formatting corrections.

The refusal added for a channel being destroyed invoked the application
callback unconditionally.  An application whose callback responds to failure
by starting a replacement lookup -- an ordinary retry pattern, since
ARES_EDESTRUCTION is just another failure status -- re-entered the refusal
from inside the notification without bound and exhausted the stack, roughly
ten thousand frames in.  Notify only when not already inside such a
notification, which bounds it at one frame.  A nested request's argument is
no longer handed back; ares_destroy.3 says so rather than promising the
notification unconditionally.

ares_send_query_int() re-checked its query after ares_open_connection() but
not the server it captured beforehand, and the same three pieces of
application code that can free the query can free the server:
ares_set_servers_csv() from any of them destroys the servers the new
configuration omits.  Revalidate the server there, and inside
ares_open_connection() after its own two callbacks, where conn->server is
dereferenced immediately afterwards by ares_conn_set_self_ip().
ares_server_in_channel() becomes non-static for the second site.

The liveness guards tested a query id plus pointer identity.  That has the
residual case the serial was introduced to remove -- a replacement lookup is
often allocated at the address the freed one had, and may be handed the same
16-bit id -- so they now compare query->serial through a single
ares_query_is_live() helper.  The pre-existing id check at the end of
ares_send_query() gets the same treatment; it previously tested only for
NULL, so a reissued id made it report success for a query that had ended.

Also: the two array destroys in ares_destroy() were dead, since the leave
above already flushed and freed both queues; five overlapping comment blocks
in the test file are collapsed to the one that is true; and the test's
errno/fcntl includes no longer nest a _WIN32 guard inside a WIN32 one.

Signed-off-by: Brad House <brad@brad-house.com>

* defer reclamation of servers and connections across library calls

Six Majors across three review rounds, and three published CVEs before them,
are one defect: a library-owned object freed by application code while the
library still holds a pointer to it.  CVE-2025-31498 fixed it at one call
site; CVE-2025-62408 was "a missed case from CVE-2025-31498"; CVE-2026-33630
covered "the remaining occurrences of the pattern" for queries.  The server
and connection half has never had a mechanism, only point guards, and each
round of review has found another site.

Callbacks split cleanly in two.  Notification callbacks -- the query
callback, socket-state and server-state -- return nothing the library needs,
so their delivery is already deferred to a safe point, and that half has
produced no findings since.  The I/O hooks -- the socket-open function from
ares_set_socket_functions_ex(), and the ares_set_socket_callback() and
ares_set_socket_configure_callback() callbacks -- cannot be deferred, because
their return value is needed to continue.  They run inside half-constructed
state and may reconfigure the servers, which frees them.

So defer the destruction instead of the call.  ares_close_connection() and
ares_destroy_server() still unlink from every lookup structure immediately --
nothing can find a torn-down object, ares_server_in_channel() reports it gone
and ares_slist_node_find() does not return it -- but while a library call is
in progress the memory is put on a pending list and freed by the flush that
already delivers deferred notifications, once the outermost call is
unwinding.  A pointer captured before a hook therefore stays readable for the
rest of that call.

The existing revalidation checks stay, because they are still needed for
semantics: a removed server must not be selected, written to or have its
failure count adjusted.  What changes is that missing one is now "acted on a
server that was removed" rather than a use-after-free.

Teardown becomes idempotent.  Once a connection can outlive its own close,
reaching ares_close_connection() twice is ordinary -- handle_conn_error()
after a failed write does exactly that -- and doing the work twice would
requeue queries that have already moved and put the connection on the pending
list a second time, which is a double free.  ARES_CONN_FLAG_DEAD makes the
second call a no-op.  This was found by testing this change, not by review.

Verified with three reproducers using only the public API, under
AddressSanitizer, each run with reclamation enabled and disabled:

  configure hook reconfigures servers   ares_conn_connect()      UAF -> clean
  send function reconfigures servers    handle_conn_error()      UAF -> clean
  socket-create hook reconfigures       ares_conn_set_self_ip()  UAF -> clean

Test: ReconfigureInConfigureHookNoUseAfterFree, which is a heap-use-after-free
in ares_conn_connect() with reclamation disabled.  It also asserts the query
completes rather than being stranded.

Known limit: this protects payloads, not container nodes.  ares_slist_node_
destroy() still frees the node, so the re-read-the-head iteration discipline
and the servers_generation counter remain necessary.

* review round 7: harden teardown ordering, fix a leak, correct docs

The idempotence flag is set as soon as the connection is unlinked rather than
at the end of teardown.  ares_requeue_queries() runs in between and ends
queries terminally once their retries are exhausted, which invokes the
application's callback; with the flag set afterwards, a second
ares_close_connection() arriving in that window would run the body again,
close the descriptor twice and list the connection for reclamation twice.
Not reachable today -- after the unlink nothing can obtain the connection but
frames already on the stack, which run later -- but it now holds by
construction.  It also gives ares_close_sockets() its termination condition:
that loop re-reads the head and relies on the close unlinking the node, so a
dead connection on the list would spin with the channel lock held.  Asserted.

redundant, and that was wrong for one path: if the first insert into a
freshly created queue fails, the array is left allocated and empty, the flush
loop never runs because both queues are empty, and nothing else frees it.
The suite drives allocation failure and CI runs it under valgrind.

land on main, which releases as 1.35.0 -- docs/ares_set_query_enqueue_cb.3
already carries a 1.35.0 note for a function that exists only there.  All
four now name both.

ares_set_servers_csv.3 gains a REENTRANCY section.  Three of the four manual
pages this series touches tell the reader a callback may call the server
configuration functions; the page they would then read said nothing about
what a nested call does.  Last writer wins, and the outer call returns
success without its own list surviving, which an application cannot otherwise
discover.

Also: the socket-state message's readable and writable are ares_bool_t rather
than int, converted at the callback which takes ints; and four tests left
CancelInCbData::cbs uninitialised while the callback incremented it.

GHSA-6WFJ-RWM7-3542.1fa3b86a0b8d18fe7b60f3228a01d770feb026bc:
Merge commit from fork

* Fix double-free in process_timeouts() when ares_cancel() called from callback

Detach query from queries_by_qid and all_queries before invoking
callback to prevent ares_cancel() from finding and double-freeing it.

This applies the same requeue pattern used in read_answers() to
process_timeouts().

* Consolidate requeue handling: fix #1043 recursion and complete the double-free fix

The prior commit fixed the process_timeouts() double-free (GHSA-6wfj-rwm7-3542 /
CVE-2026-33630) by deferring callbacks and detaching the query before invoking
it.  However:

  1. The identical double-free is reachable through read_answers(): its deferred
     ENDQUERY flush invoked the callback without first detaching the query from
     queries_by_qid / all_queries, so a reentrant ares_cancel() from a *normal*
     response callback frees the query and read_answers() frees it again.  The
     advisory's premise that read_answers() was already safe holds only for
     cross-query cancellation, not self-cancellation.

  2. Issue #1043 (unbounded ares_requeue_query() -> ares_send_query() recursion
     leading to stack overflow) was still present: ares_send_query() and the
     read_answers()/process_timeouts() flushes re-dispatched retries by calling
     ares_send_query() directly rather than iteratively.

Both problems share one root cause: work that must be deferred was instead done
immediately.  This change funnels every flush site through a single helper,
ares_flush_requeue(), which:

  - re-dispatches retries by appending to the same list and looping (via the new
    internal ares_send_query_int()), so retryable failures iterate instead of
    recursing, and
  - fully detaches each query (ares_detach_query()) before invoking its callback,
    so a reentrant ares_cancel() can never find and double-free it.

ares_send_query() becomes a thin wrapper that drives ares_send_query_int() and
drains the list.  Because a deferred retry can terminally fail (and free the
query) while draining, the wrapper reports the query's real fate by checking
whether it is still tracked, rather than dereferencing the possibly-freed query.

read_answers(), process_timeouts(), and process_answer()'s EDNS-rewrite-failure
path now all defer through this helper, removing two duplicated inline flush
loops.

Regression tests (test/ares-test-mock.cc):
  - HighRetryNoStackOverflow: a large retry count with always-failing socket
    creation overflows the stack on unpatched code and completes iteratively
    with the fix.
  - CancelInCallbackNoDoubleFree: calling ares_cancel() from a normal response
    callback double-frees on unpatched code (ASan) and is clean with the fix.
